title: Consistency Regularised Gradient Flows for Inverse Problems
claim: Naive prior sampling gives wrong reconstructions; jointly optimizing the prompt while flowing samples corrects them in few iterations.
layout: 2 rows, left-to-right arrows, red-vs-blue borders for wrong/correct outputs
description: A blurry, motion-blurred toddler face labeled 'Observation y' sits at the far left. The top row shows two reconstructions of that face. On the left, 'Incorrect CWGF recon.' has a red border and visible cat-whisker artifacts. On the right, 'CWGF recon.' has a blue border and is clean and sharp. Three arrows between them are labeled 'Wasserstein-2 gradient flow, iterations 1→16'. The bottom row shows prior samples. 'Prior sample at step 1' is a cat photo, and 'Prior sample at step 16' is a human face. Arrows between them are labeled 'Prompt optimisation, iterations 1→16'. Dashed arrows labeled 'used by CWGF' point from each prior sample up to the matching reconstruction. Prompt boxes sit underneath: a red box reads 'a photo of a cat' and a blue box reads 'optimized c*(y)'. The eye goes first to the faces, then to the red and blue contrast.
caption: Our Euclidean-Wasserstein flow jointly optimizes the text prompt and yields accurate posterior samples in few NFEs. Zoom in for fine details.
abstract: Vision-Language Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) (Rombach et al., 2022) provide powerful generative priors for inverse problems. However, existing LDM-based inverse solvers typically require a large number of neural function evaluations (NFEs) and backpropagation through large pretrained components, leading to substantial computational costs and, in some cases, degraded reconstruction quality. We propose a unified Euclidean-Wasserstein-2 gradient-flow framework that jointly performs posterior sampling and prompt optimization in the latent space through a single flow that aligns the prior and posterior with the observed data. Combined with few-step latent text-to-image models, this formulation enables low-NFE inference without backpropagation through autoencoders. Experiments across several canonical imaging inverse problems show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly reduced computational cost.
